1:
The summons is heard before anything is seen, and its phrasing is contested. Calvin reads it as a command, since taking the noun otherwise forces the rendering visitations and yields no sense from a prefecture of the city drawing near. Keil and Delitzsch reject it too, punishments not suiting a context that introduces the men who execute them. Henry keeps it and makes a play of it, the visitors of the city being at hand for a people who would not know their day of visitation in mercy. Ellicott hears the raised voice as the natural expression of indignation.

Who the six are divides the chapter. Ellicott denies they can be earthly officers: the phrase every man is used constantly of angels, and the vision plainly presents angelic executioners. Henry agrees, putting the Chaldean armies below them as tools; angels once charged to guard the city now have charge to waste it. Clarke takes them for the Chaldeans and reads the party as an eastern monarch's seven counsellors, the one with the inkhorn being the minister who kept the book of death and the book of life. Calvin also finds the Chaldeans indicated, the north gate being the direct way from Babylon. Gill and Wesley leave it open, Gill reporting the rabbinic identification with six named generals, Wesley preferring angels with an instrument each, sword, pestilence, famine.

Why six is asked and mostly unanswered. Calvin says he has not found out, dismisses the attempt to derive it from a list of enemy leaders elsewhere as varying and forced, and offers only that God may have wished to show a small band sufficient, breaking the pride of a people who assumed a great force would be needed. Henry counts one for each principal gate and compares Sodom, which had two destroying angels where this city has six. Ellicott counts differently, making the man in linen a seventh and completing a mystical number.

The man with the inkhorn is described and then left unidentified. Ellicott has him among the six but not of them, unarmed where they are armed, in the priestly dress, which is worn elsewhere simply as a mark of purity, so that no priestly character need be inferred. He refuses both identifications in circulation, with the Babylonian god of writing and with Christ, since nothing in the text gives the figure any identity: he is an angelic messenger sent to mark the faithful, and no more. Clarke makes him a court officer instead. On the moving of the glory Ellicott finds two ideas blended: the order for judgment issues from the very house men looked to as their pledge of safety, and the Lord has begun to leave it. Gill takes the movement as proof that a divine Person is meant.

The mark produces the sharpest split. Keil and Delitzsch render it a cross, the word being the last letter of the alphabet. Ellicott agrees and presses it: in the script the Hebrews used up to that time, and kept on their coins long after, the letter had the form of a cross, which is why the older Christian writers made so much of it and why the Church came to sign the baptized. Clarke knows all of it, the Latin version's sign thau, the old opinion, the shape on Samaritan coins, and rejects the inference. The Hebrew says only that a mark shall be made, with no word as to what it was; it does what the blood on the doorposts did, telling the destroying angel which house to pass; and since the whole passed in vision we are bound to no letter or figure. He concludes that the symbol teaches only that God distinguishes the penitent from the hardened. Ellicott ends at the same point from the other side: the marking regards character only, taking no notice of birth or position.
5:
Calvin enters the argument about the mark only to dismiss it. The word means simply a mark, and nothing compels anyone to make it the last letter; the notion that the pious were signed with it because the word for the law begins with that letter he calls puerile, and Jerome's report that the Samaritans of his day wrote it as a cross he calls a figment and plainly nugatory. If puzzles must be had, he offers a better one in jest: the faithful might be marked with the last letter, being last among men. His serious point is that when everything seems turned upside down God never lays aside the care of his own, angels being the ministers of that protection.

The execution is immediate and without exception. Ellicott allows no interval: judgment waits only until those mercy will spare are secured, as it waited for the rescue of Lot, and then falls utterly. He takes it for one of many passages where God reveals himself as taking vengeance at last, without pity, on those who rejected his long-suffering; the revelation of future wrath, he insists, is no less clear than that of love. Henry presses the absence of exception harder: neither the beauty of the virgins nor the innocency of the babes secures them. Sparing whom God has doomed, he adds, is doing God's work deceitfully, and no one needs to be more merciful than God.

Beginning at the sanctuary draws two explanations. Clarke makes it a rule of proportion: those who sinned against the most mercy and privilege are the first victims, the unfaithful within the church punished most; but he turns at once on anyone outside who might enjoy it, since if judgment begins at the house of God the end of those who obey not the gospel is worse, while the truly penitent of every description are safe. Henry gives the causal reason: the wickedness began there, the debaucheries of the priests poisoning the springs to which all the corruption of the streams was owing, so the slaughter begins where the offence did, to see whether the people will take warning from the judgment on their priests. Neither the sacredness of the place nor a man's eminence shelters him.

The order to defile the house divides them on what the defiling amounts to. Clarke hears a dreadful sentence: the house is given to pollution because God will no longer dwell in it. Ellicott explains that under the older economy the touch of a dead body was the utmost pollution possible, so the temple might have been expected to escape it; but justice overrides such technicalities, as when a man was killed at the altar itself; and here the defilement is part of the judgment. Gill makes it an instruction not to hesitate for fear of defiling the place, since those who defiled it with abominations may now defile it with their blood. Henry alone draws the opposite conclusion, that acts of necessary justice were, whatever they were ceremonially, a purification rather than a pollution, since they put away evil.

Calvin meets an objection. It was polluted already, someone will say, and he grants it; but the word regards how the people perceived the matter. They had infected the place and still boasted that the worship and the name remained there. A corpse or a dog in the sanctuary they would have cried out upon as portentous, while they walked in loaded with blood, rapine and perjury and counted that pollution nothing; the command derides the sloth by promising a house so full of corpses that they will at last admit it is no longer holy. He adds that the siege had probably not begun, likely enough since the threatenings were thought fabulous, and that the point of showing the destroyers already waiting is that when the hour came the army would be ready.
8:
The words saying the prophet was left are handled as a textual problem and as a picture. Keil and Delitzsch judge the written form incongruous, a participle and an imperfect fused into one and plainly a copyist's slip; rather than emend it to the first person they read it as a participle continuing the circumstantial clause. Calvin takes the oddity as meaningful, noting that the word looks compounded of two tenses, or of the first person and the third, and finding no ambiguity in the sense whatever the grammar: the destroyers had left none, so the man seemed to himself to stand alone, snatched from a burning meant to consume all. Ellicott gives the scene rather than the form: the courts lately thronged with idolaters in the full confidence of their sin are now a city of the dead, and he stands alone in the middle of it.

Calvin answers the obvious objection, that not everybody was killed. The slaughter nearly destroyed the name of the people, and those who survived were as good as dead, exile being worse to them than dying; the vision also carries the threat out to the last penalty that waits on the ungodly. So the ruin was shown as though every citizen had perished, to make plain how terrible a thing was pressing on a people that feared nothing. Clarke keeps to the recorded dead, the elders, the twenty-five who worshipped the sun and the women who wept for Tammuz, and dates the outcry to the sight of them falling.

The answer is read as a correction of the prophet as much as a defence of God. Calvin says it restrains an excess of fervour and asserts the equity of the judgment against the opinions that creep over us whenever God's judgments do not answer our will. He is careful about the tone: the prophet expostulates, but suppliantly, submitting his senses to the command, which is why an answer capable of calming him is given at all. Other prophets take similar liberties, and his account of them is that they return directly to themselves. Ellicott hears only sternness in the reply, with no room for any mitigation of the sentence.

The charge provoking it is the saying that the Lord has forsaken the land. Clarke gives the phrase its narrower sense, this land, and unpacks what they meant: he has abandoned the place, neither sees nor cares, and can no longer be an object of worship here. What God resents, on Clarke's reading, is that it reduces him to an idol or a provincial deity with authority in one district. He answers the second half just as sharply on the following verse: they say the Lord does not see, which is false, for the eye that has seen all their abominations is the eye that will neither pity nor spare. Gill puts the ground of the sentence in what they did rather than said: they had not spared the poor and needy, the widow and the fatherless, but perverted judgment and shed innocent blood.

The chapter ends with a report, and the readers make more of it than its length suggests. Ellicott observes that nothing has been said of those to be saved, they being too few to affect the impression the vision leaves; but they are not forgotten, and the report of the man in linen is put there to show it. Clarke draws the same comfort and a warning with it: angels and men alike must give account, for though God is everywhere and sees everything they must still answer personally; and the account rendered here is that the penitents are all signed and safe, good news for those who mourn. Gill notes that the Syriac reads then I saw the man, directing the prophet to call to mind the distinguishing goodness of God towards his own.
